title: Tabs, spaces and Vim: developer holy wars, measured
description: Developers have argued about tabs versus spaces and Vim versus Emacs for decades, and now and then someone collects data. Each Question takes one argument, shows what a survey, a traffic log or a tool's design actually measured, and asks what you can and can't conclude. You'll also leave knowing how to quit Vim.
author: Quizbun

questions.title: In Stack Overflow's 2017 Developer Survey, which group of professional developers reported the higher median salary: tabs users or spaces users?

options.text: Spaces users, by about $15,000 a year
Tabs users, by about $15,000 a year
Neither: the two medians were within $1,000 of each other
The survey didn't ask about salary, so nobody knows

questions.explanation:
The data scientist David Robinson compared the two groups in the 2017 survey data. Developers who indented with spaces reported a median salary of **$59,140**; those who used tabs reported **$43,750**.

A gap that size between two groups that differ only in a keystroke should make you suspicious rather than excited. A raw median mixes everything together: country, experience, language, job type. If spaces happened to be more common in higher-paying countries or languages, a gap would appear even if indentation had nothing to do with pay. The next Questions look at how Robinson tried to separate those effects.

Also note what kind of evidence this is: self-reported salaries from people who chose to take a survey on Stack Overflow.
questions.references: [Stack Overflow Blog: Developers who use spaces make more money than those who use tabs (David Robinson, 2017)](https://stackoverflow.blog/2017/06/15/developers-use-spaces-make-money-use-tabs/), [GitHub: dgrtwo/tabs-spaces-post (the analysis code)](https://github.com/dgrtwo/tabs-spaces-post)

questions.title: How did the 28,657 professional developers who answered the 2017 indentation question split between tabs, spaces and both?

options.text: Close to a tie: about 41% spaces, 41% tabs, and 18% both
Spaces won easily: about 80% spaces and 20% tabs
Tabs won easily: about 70% tabs and 30% spaces
About a third each for tabs, spaces and both

questions.explanation:
The split was **41.8% spaces, 40.7% tabs and 17.5% both**. Nobody won the holy war; the two camps were almost exactly the same size.

That near-tie matters for the salary comparison. Both groups are large, so the salary gap isn't the product of one tiny, unusual group. Of the 28,657 who answered the indentation question, 12,426 also reported a salary, and those are the people the salary analysis rests on.

The "both" group is a reminder that survey categories flatten real behavior. Many developers use whatever the project's style guide or formatter says, which can mean tabs in one repository and spaces in the next.
questions.references: [Stack Overflow Blog: Developers who use spaces make more money than those who use tabs (David Robinson, 2017)](https://stackoverflow.blog/2017/06/15/developers-use-spaces-make-money-use-tabs/)

images.alt: Bar chart of the 2017 Stack Overflow survey question on indentation, 28,657 professional developers. Spaces 41.8%, tabs 40.7%, both 17.5%, also shown as a single stacked bar. A note says tabs and spaces are nearly tied and about one developer in six uses both.
images.caption: Percentages from David Robinson's 2017 Stack Overflow analysis. Chart drawn for this Quiz.

questions.title: To test whether the salary gap was just a side effect of other differences, Robinson fitted a regression model. Which factors did it control for?

options.text: Country
Years of programming experience
Programming language and type of developer
Level of formal education
Company size
The editor or IDE each developer uses
Hours worked per week

questions.explanation:
Robinson's linear regression included country, years of programming experience, developer type and language (49 categories), formal education, open source contribution, hobby programming and company size, alongside tabs versus spaces. Editor and hours worked weren't in the model.

Controlling for a factor means comparing like with like: a spaces user and a tabs user in the same country, with the same experience, writing the same language. After those adjustments, using spaces was still **associated with an 8.6% higher salary** (95% confidence interval roughly 6% to 10.4%). Robinson noted that this is about the same difference as 2.4 extra years of experience, and the gap showed up in every subgroup he examined.

So the obvious explanations, such as "spaces users are in the US" or "spaces users write better-paid languages", don't account for it. That still leaves every factor nobody measured, which is the subject of the next Question.
questions.references: [Stack Overflow Blog: Developers who use spaces make more money than those who use tabs (David Robinson, 2017)](https://stackoverflow.blog/2017/06/15/developers-use-spaces-make-money-use-tabs/), [GitHub: dgrtwo/tabs-spaces-post (the analysis code)](https://github.com/dgrtwo/tabs-spaces-post)

questions.title: A colleague reads the tabs-versus-spaces result and switches their editor to spaces, expecting a raise. What does the evidence actually support?

options.text: Something that goes along with using spaces also goes along with higher pay, and the data can't say what that something is
Using spaces causes higher pay, because the model controlled for the important factors
Tabs users are worse programmers, which is why they earn less
Nothing at all: 12,426 salaries is too small a sample to find any pattern

questions.explanation:
The survey is **observational**: nobody was assigned to tabs or spaces. It can show that two things occur together, but not which one drives the other, or whether a third factor drives both. Robinson himself wrote that correlation isn't causation and that you can never be sure you've controlled for every confounding factor.

A confounder here would be anything linked to both indentation and pay that the model didn't include. Some candidates, offered as hypotheses rather than findings: working at a company that enforces a style guide or an automatic formatter, working on teams with more mature tooling, or the kind of project a developer works on. Any of these could make spaces more likely *and* pay higher, with no effect of one on the other.

The sample isn't the problem. With over 12,000 salaries, the association is very unlikely to be chance. Precision tells you the pattern is real; it can't tell you why it exists. The test that would settle causation, randomly assigning developers to tabs or spaces and waiting for their salaries, isn't going to happen.
questions.references: [Stack Overflow Blog: Developers who use spaces make more money than those who use tabs (David Robinson, 2017)](https://stackoverflow.blog/2017/06/15/developers-use-spaces-make-money-use-tabs/), [Wikipedia: Confounding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Confounding)

questions.title: You're in Vim, you've made changes you don't want, and you want out. Type a command that quits without saving.
questions.description: Assume you've already pressed Esc. Type the command exactly as you'd type it into Vim, without pressing Enter.
questions.explanation:
**`:q!`** does it. The colon moves Vim from Normal mode into Command-line mode, `q` means quit, and `!` means "I know there are unsaved changes; throw them away". Press Enter to run it. `:qa!` does the same for every open window, and **`ZQ`**, typed in Normal mode with no colon, is a shortcut for `:q!`.

Why doesn't plain `:q` work? It refuses when the buffer has changes and shows *No write since last change (add ! to override)*. That message is the safety net working: the `!` is how you tell Vim the data loss is deliberate.

Most people get stuck one step earlier. Vim starts in **Normal mode**, where letters are commands, so typing `quit` runs a sequence of editing commands instead of quitting. If you're not sure which mode you're in, press Esc. It always brings you back to Normal mode.

Case matters here. `ZQ` quits, but `zq` doesn't. Lowercase `z` starts a different family of commands, mostly for folding and scrolling.

Try it now: run `vim` in a terminal, press `i`, type something, press Esc, then type `:q!` and press Enter.

images.alt: State diagram of Vim's modes. Normal mode in the middle. Keys i, a or o go from Normal to Insert, and Esc goes back. A colon goes from Normal to Command-line, and Esc cancels back. From Normal, ZZ saves and closes and ZQ discards and closes. From Command-line, :wq then Enter saves and closes, and :q! then Enter discards and closes. A note says plain :q refuses when there are unsaved changes.
images.caption: Diagram drawn for this Quiz from Vim's `:help` documentation.

questions.title: This time you want to keep your edits. Type a Vim command that saves the file and quits.
questions.description: Again, assume you've pressed Esc, and leave out the final Enter.
questions.explanation:
**`:wq`** writes the file (`w`) and then quits (`q`). Commands in Vim's Command-line mode compose like that.

Two shortcuts do almost the same thing. **`:x`** and **`ZZ`** (Normal mode, no colon) write the file only if it has changed, then quit. The difference is subtle but real: `:wq` always writes, which updates the file's modification time even when nothing changed. That can make build tools like `make` think the file needs rebuilding. `:x` leaves an unchanged file alone.

If the write fails, for example because the file is read-only or the buffer has no name yet, Vim doesn't quit, so you can't lose work by accident. Give the buffer a name with `:w filename`, then quit.

As with `ZQ`, case matters: `ZZ` saves and quits, but `zz` just scrolls the current line to the middle of the screen.

questions.title: The Stack Overflow question "How to exit the Vim editor?" was asked in 2012. When did Stack Overflow announce it had helped one million developers?

options.text: 2012, within months of being asked

questions.explanation:
Stack Overflow published the milestone in **May 2017**, nearly five years after the question was asked in August 2012.

The traffic didn't arrive at once. Robinson's chart shows the question got little attention at first, then grew for about two years as it climbed search engine rankings, and then held roughly steady. That shape is typical for evergreen questions: a search engine sends a steady stream of new people who hit the same problem, and the counter keeps ticking.

For scale, the question accounted for about 0.005% of all Stack Overflow question traffic, or one visit in every 20,000. That sounds tiny until you remember how much traffic Stack Overflow gets.
questions.references: [Stack Overflow Blog: Stack Overflow: Helping one million developers exit Vim (David Robinson, 2017)](https://stackoverflow.blog/2017/05/23/stack-overflow-helping-one-million-developers-exit-vim/), [Stack Overflow: How do I exit Vim?](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/11828270/how-do-i-exit-vim)

questions.title: Guess: at weekday peak hours in 2017, about how many people an hour visited Stack Overflow to find out how to exit Vim?
questions.description: Enter a whole number. Answers within 20 of the reported figure count.
questions.explanation:
Robinson reported **about 80 people an hour** during weekday peak hours. That's more than one person a minute, stuck in an editor with no visible way out.

The number measures page visits, not unique people or people who were actually trapped. Some visitors were curious, some came back more than once, and some were stuck in Vim over SSH on another machine. "Visits to a help page" is a *proxy* for "people who got stuck", and a good analysis states which one it counted, as Robinson's does.

The weekday peak is its own clue. If the traffic follows working hours, most of these people were probably stuck at work, in the middle of something else, which is where the next Questions go.
questions.references: [Stack Overflow Blog: Stack Overflow: Helping one million developers exit Vim (David Robinson, 2017)](https://stackoverflow.blog/2017/05/23/stack-overflow-helping-one-million-developers-exit-vim/)

questions.title: Among visitors to Vim questions on Stack Overflow, developers from which group were the most likely to be looking for the exit?
questions.description: Robinson grouped visitors by the tags they visited most and compared how often each group's Vim traffic went to the exit question.

options.text: Front-end web developers, such as those who visit jQuery, CSS and AngularJS questions
Microsoft developers, such as those who visit C# and SQL Server questions
C and C++ developers
Python and Ruby developers

questions.explanation:
**Front-end web developers** were the most likely to be looking for the exit. Microsoft developers (C#, SQL Server) and mobile developers (Android, iOS) came next. C, C++, Python and Ruby developers were the *least* likely.

Look at how the metric is built. It isn't "how many front-end developers exist". It's the share of each group's Vim-question visits that went to the exit question. That ratio corrects for group size: a huge group with no Vim problems still scores low. Without that normalization, the ranking would mostly reflect which technologies have the most developers.

The same analysis found country differences, with Ukraine, Turkey and Indonesia high and China, Korea and Japan low. The post read the low scores as people who open Vim on purpose and already know how to leave.
questions.references: [Stack Overflow Blog: Stack Overflow: Helping one million developers exit Vim (David Robinson, 2017)](https://stackoverflow.blog/2017/05/23/stack-overflow-helping-one-million-developers-exit-vim/)

questions.title: What is the most plausible reason front-end developers got stuck in Vim more often than C or Python developers?

options.text: They mostly work in IDEs, so they meet Vim by accident, for example when a Git command opens it
Front-end work requires editing files in Vim more often
Vim can't open JavaScript or CSS files correctly
Front-end developers make more typos, which trigger Vim's modes

questions.explanation:
Robinson's reading is that front-end developers usually work in an IDE or a graphical editor, while C, C++, Python and Ruby developers more often work in plain text editors, including Vim itself. Someone who chose Vim knows how to leave it. Someone who was *dropped into* Vim by another tool doesn't.

Note the status of this claim. The data shows *which groups* visit the exit question; the "IDE users arrive by accident" story is an interpretation that fits the pattern, not something the traffic logs measured directly. It's plausible, and it matches the country pattern too, but it's an explanation, not a finding.

The other options don't hold up. Vim opens any text file, including JavaScript and CSS, and nothing about front-end work needs Vim. The question is how people end up there without choosing to.
questions.references: [Stack Overflow Blog: Stack Overflow: Helping one million developers exit Vim (David Robinson, 2017)](https://stackoverflow.blog/2017/05/23/stack-overflow-helping-one-million-developers-exit-vim/)

questions.title: You run `git commit` without `-m` on a machine where you've never configured an editor, and a Vim screen appears. Why?

options.text: Git needs an editor for the commit message and, when none is configured, falls back to a compile-time default that is usually `vi`
Git ships its own built-in copy of Vim and always uses it for commit messages
Your terminal opens Vim whenever a program asks for multi-line input
Git detected an error in your commit and opened Vim so you could fix it

questions.explanation:
Without `-m`, Git opens an editor so you can write the commit message. To pick one, it checks, in order: the `GIT_EDITOR` environment variable, the `core.editor` config setting, `VISUAL`, `EDITOR`, and finally the default chosen when Git was compiled, **which is usually `vi`**. On many systems `vi` launches Vim.

So nothing went wrong. Every setting was empty and Git used the last fallback. The same thing happens with `git merge` when it asks for a merge message and with `git rebase -i`.

If you're already in Vim: type your message, press Esc, then `:wq`. To save and exit without committing, leave the message empty; Git aborts a commit with an empty message.

To avoid it next time, set an editor you know. For VS Code:

```bash
git config --global core.editor "code --wait"
```

`--wait` matters: without it, the `code` command returns immediately, and Git sees an empty message.
questions.references: [Git documentation: git-var, GIT_EDITOR](https://git-scm.com/docs/git-var), [Git documentation: git-commit](https://git-scm.com/docs/git-commit), [VS Code docs: Source control in VS Code](https://code.visualstudio.com/docs/sourcecontrol/overview)

images.alt: A list of five steps Git checks to choose an editor: 1 GIT_EDITOR environment variable, 2 core.editor git config setting, 3 VISUAL environment variable, 4 EDITOR environment variable, each marked 'not set? go down'. Step 5, highlighted, is vi, the default chosen when Git was compiled. A note says on many systems vi is Vim, and you often land in it from git commit without -m, git merge, or git rebase -i.
images.caption: Order of preference from the Git documentation for `git var GIT_EDITOR`. Diagram drawn for this Quiz.

questions.title: Why does vi, and Vim after it, use modes where single letters are commands, instead of letting you type text right away?

options.text: vi was built in the 1970s for slow terminals, where short commands let you work faster than the screen could redraw
Terminals at the time had no Ctrl or Alt keys, so letters were the only way to send commands
Modes saved disk space by storing commands as single bytes
Bill Joy copied the design from Emacs

questions.explanation:
vi comes from a line of Unix editors: Ken Thompson's **ed** (1969), George Coulouris's **em**, and Bill Joy's **ex**, of which vi is the visual mode. ed was famously terse, reporting most errors with a single `?`, because it ran on teletypes over slow connections.

Joy wrote vi over a **300 baud modem**, about 30 characters a second. He explained that the terse single-character commands, and the ability to type ahead of the display, came from that limit: he wanted to keep working while the screen painted slower than he could think. When one keystroke means "delete a word", you send one character instead of a long command.

His terminal, a Lear Siegler ADM-3A, explains two more quirks. Its Escape key sat where Tab is on today's keyboards, so switching modes took one easy reach. And `h`, `j`, `k`, `l` had arrows printed on them, because the terminal had no separate arrow keys. That's why they still move the cursor in Vim.

The terminals had Ctrl keys, and Emacs's chord-based design is the opposite approach, not the source of vi's.
questions.references: [Wikipedia: vi (text editor)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vi_(text_editor)), [Wikipedia: ed (text editor)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_(text_editor)), [The Register: Bill Joy's greatest gift to man, the vi editor (2003)](https://www.theregister.com/2003/09/11/bill_joys_greatest_gift/)

questions.title: Richard Stallman's parody Church of Emacs calls vi "the editor of the beast". Where does the name come from?

options.text: "vi vi vi" read as Roman numerals is 6 6 6, the number of the beast
vi was the sixth editor released for Unix, in version 6
vi's source code was 666 lines long
vi's first release was on 6 June 1966

questions.explanation:
In Roman numerals, VI is 6, so **vi-vi-vi reads as 6-6-6**, the number of the beast. The joke belongs to the Church of Emacs, a parody religion Stallman created. He appears in it as **Saint IGNUcius**, wearing a robe and a halo made from an old disk platter.

The church's real target isn't vi. Its sermon is about software freedom: using a free version of vi is described as a penance rather than a sin, and the sin is proprietary software.

The editor war itself is one of the original holy wars of Usenet, with recorded flame wars going back to at least 1985. vi users hit back with their own jokes about Emacs, which uses long Ctrl and Meta key chords. None of it was ever settled by data, which is part of why it could run for decades.

questions.title: In the 2025 Stack Overflow Developer Survey, 75.9% of respondents said they regularly used VS Code, 24.3% Vim and 14% Neovim, while Emacs appeared only as a write-in answer, at 0.15%. Which conclusions does this data support?
questions.description: The question was "Which development environments and AI-enabled code editing tools did you use regularly over the past year?", with "check all that apply". About 26,000 people answered it.

options.text: VS Code was the most used development environment among these respondents
Many respondents used more than one editor
About one respondent in four said they used Vim regularly
Emacs is used by fewer than 1 developer in 500
Vim's share has shrunk since 2017, because VS Code took its users
These percentages describe all professional developers worldwide

questions.explanation:
Three conclusions hold. VS Code led clearly, for the fourth year running. About a quarter of respondents checked Vim. And because respondents could check every tool they used, the percentages add up to far more than 100%: VS Code alone is 75.9%, and Visual Studio, Notepad++, IntelliJ IDEA and Vim each got another 24% to 29%. Many people use VS Code *and* Vim, for example Vim for quick edits over SSH.

The other three don't follow:

- **Emacs at 0.15%** is an artifact of the form. It wasn't a listed option, so the only way to count it was to type it in, and most people don't bother. Unlisted answers are always undercounted, so this number tells you almost nothing about Emacs.
- **A trend** needs data from several years collected the same way. One year's snapshot can't show that Vim lost users, and it certainly can't show *why*.
- **All developers**: respondents chose to take a survey promoted by Stack Overflow. That's a large sample, but not a random one.
questions.references: [Stack Overflow Developer Survey 2025: Technology, Dev IDEs](https://survey.stackoverflow.co/2025/technology), [Stack Overflow Developer Survey 2025: Methodology](https://survey.stackoverflow.co/2025/methodology)

questions.title: Guess the year: when did Bill Joy build the visual mode of the ex editor that became vi?
questions.description: Enter a year. Answers within one year of it count.
questions.explanation:
Joy, then a graduate student at UC Berkeley, added a full-screen visual mode to ex in **1976–1977**. Sources date it differently: Wikipedia's summary says 1976, and the ex source code history points to a redesign from June to October 1977. That's why answers from 1976 to 1978 count.

The release history is just as layered, a useful reminder that "when was X invented?" often has several honest answers:

- **March 1978**: ex 1.1 shipped in the first Berkeley Software Distribution (1BSD).
- **May 1979**: ex 2.0 in 2BSD installed the program under the name `vi`, starting straight in visual mode. vi and ex are the same program.
- **1991**: Bram Moolenaar completed Vim 1.14, its first public release, distributed on an Amiga Fish Disk in January 1992.

So Vim's modes are close to 50 years old, and the question of how to leave them is older than most of the developers asking it.

questions.title: Looking back across the Quiz, which of these claims does the evidence support?

options.text: In 2017 survey data, spaces users reported higher salaries than tabs users, even after controlling for country, experience and language
Among visitors to Vim questions, front-end developers were more likely than C developers to be looking for the exit
With no editor configured, Git usually falls back to `vi`
Switching from tabs to spaces will raise your salary
Front-end developers are less skilled programmers than C developers
Most developers use Vim as their main editor

questions.explanation:
The three supported claims each stay inside what was measured:

- **The salary gap** is a real association in self-reported survey data, and it survived controls for the obvious confounders. It's still an association.
- **The Vim ranking** compares the share of each group's Vim traffic that went to the exit question. It measures confusion about one editor, not programming skill. The "they use IDEs and land in Vim by accident" story is a plausible interpretation on top of that.
- **Git's fallback** isn't data at all. It's documented design, so you can check it directly with `git var GIT_EDITOR`.

The three unsupported claims each take one step too far. "Switch and earn more" turns a correlation into a cause. "Less skilled" swaps the thing measured, finding the exit, for something it wasn't: ability. And "most developers use Vim" misreads 24.3% of one self-selected survey as a majority.

That's the pattern to take into your next holy war: ask what was actually measured, on whom, and whether anything else could explain it.
